title: Permissions in a support inbox
excerpt: Show an agent what they can do on a conversation, and the reason a refund, a reply, or a note is unavailable. A control that fails after the form is filled feels like a bug.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water, two regions that stay distinct the way a public reply and an internal note must.
caption: Two colors, one frame, and a boundary you can see. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which actions need an explanation when they are missing?
faqs.answer: Reply, refund, and anything else an agent will look for. Say who can do it, and say the cap if there is one. Hide mailbox setup and other admin acts they have no reason to expect. A button that opens a form and then says forbidden wastes the promise they may already have typed.

faqs.question: How should internal notes be protected?
faqs.answer: Keep them visually different from the public reply, and keep them out of customer email. A trainee can be allowed to note and not send, if the composer says so before they type. Shared logins make that audit impossible. Give the trainee a seat.

faqs.question: What should happen when an agent leaves?
faqs.answer: Their send right ends immediately, and their open conversations return to a queue or a named lead. Drafts should be kept or handed over on purpose. A customer must not sit inside an account nobody can open.

markdown:
Plain support inbox permissions ux shows an agent what they can do on the next conversation, and a plain reason when an action is unavailable. A hidden reply button feels like a bug. A refund control that fails after the form is filled feels like one too.

The W3C's WCAG overview organizes guidelines as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. If an agent cannot perceive the boundary, or cannot understand it, the queue will fill with retries and side channels. The server can still say no. The screen has to say why.

## Name the roles by the work

Write roles as sentences before you draw a matrix. An agent answers the next conversation and uses the tools that answer requires. A lead assigns, reads notes, and may refund within a limit. A specialist sees the queue for their topic and may not see billing. An admin seats people and connects the mailbox. A contractor sees only the conversations you assigned, and only for the weeks you named.

A useful starter set:

- Agent: reply, note, snooze, and the customer context required to answer.
- Lead: assign, reopen, and refunds up to a stated amount.
- Specialist: a filtered queue, reply, and no access to other teams' notes.
- Admin: mailboxes, seats, and the saved replies everyone shares.
- Observer: read a thread for training, send nothing.

If your company is three people, you do not need five roles. You need the sentences. Add a role when someone is blocked every day, not when the settings page looks sparse.

The customer is a role too. They can send and read what you marked public. They cannot read internal notes, and they cannot see other customers. That sounds obvious until a quoted thread or a forwarded notification includes the note. Treat outbound templates as a permissions screen.

## Reply, note, and refund

The reply box and the internal note should be visibly different, and the permission to use each can differ. A trainee might leave notes and not send. Say that in the composer. "You can leave a note. A lead sends the reply." Do not let them type a full answer into a box that will fail on submit. The limit belongs before the typing.

Refunds, cancellations, and address changes are not reply permissions. They are money and identity. If this agent cannot refund, show the order in the margin and say who can. "Refunds above $50 need a lead. Assign the conversation to the lead queue." A button that opens a form and then says forbidden has wasted the customer's time as well as the agent's, because the agent may already have promised the refund in prose.

If they can refund only up to an amount, show the amount on the control. "Refund up to $50." When the order is larger, the control should explain the cap, not disappear. Disappearing controls feel like a rendering bug. A cap is a rule. Rules can be written in a sentence.

Saved replies are shared or personal. A personal snippet should not be editable by the whole team, and a shared snippet should not be editable by a new agent on their first afternoon. Say which kind a snippet is, next to its name. The permission is part of the label.

## Seeing the customer without seeing everything

The margin can show plan, orders, and recent tickets without becoming a full customer database. Decide, per role, which fields appear. A contractor answering shipping questions needs the address and the tracking. They do not need the card's last digits or the internal lifetime value, unless those change the reply you expect them to write. If a field is absent, and the agent would look for it, leave a line. "Payment details are limited to leads." Silence makes them open another tool, and the other tool becomes the real inbox.

Other customers must never appear because a search or a related-ticket widget was greedy. "People with the same company domain" is a feature that leaks conversations across employees of a customer, and sometimes across strangers who share a host. If you ship it, scope it, and say the scope. "Other tickets from this email address." Not "other tickets that looked similar."

Assignment is a permission to concentrate attention, not a permission to hide mail. A conversation assigned to Sam can still be visible to the lead, labeled as Sam's. If agents can only see their own assignments, say so in the queue header, and give the lead a different header. Two people looking at "the inbox" should not be looking at secret subsets unless the screen admits the subset.

## Mailboxes, channels, and seats

Connecting a support address is an admin act. It pulls in other people's mail. The screen should say what will be ingested and who on the team will see it. "This will import mail sent to help@, including old mail, visible to agents and leads." A one-click connect with no sentence is how a personal inbox gets shared by mistake.

Channel accounts, a social page, a review site, follow the same rule. Name the audience of the import. If a channel is public, remind the agent that a reply may be public. The permission to reply and the visibility of the reply are different facts. Both belong on the composer. "This reply will be public on the review." Let them switch to an internal note without guessing.

Removing a seat should say what happens to assigned conversations. They return to the queue, or they move to a named lead, and open drafts are kept or handed over. Do not strand a customer inside an account nobody can open. Expired contractors should lose send immediately, and the header on any thread they still appear in should show that they are gone, so a lead does not wait for them.

Links in notification emails are permissions. A link that lets anyone who forwards it reply as the agent is too much. A link that lets the agent open the right conversation, after they sign in, is enough. If a link expires, say so. "This alert is old. Open the queue and search the customer's name." Do not dump them on a blank forbidden page with no noun.

## Coaching views are still permissions

A lead watching an agent work, or reading a queue "for quality," is a role with a tempting overreach. They need the public reply and the internal note. They do not need to send as the agent, and they do not need a hidden mode that types into the customer's thread under someone else's name. If you offer an impersonation tool for debugging, put it behind an admin action with a sentence that lands in the audit line. "Sent by Riley, acting as Sam." The customer-facing name and the internal truth can both exist. One of them must not be a secret from your own team.

Quality scores and "who used a macro" are easy to bolt onto an inbox and hard to justify to the person being measured. If a lead can see them, the agent should know they are visible. A metric collected in silence changes behavior in ways you did not design, usually toward closing tickets rather than answering them. Say what is recorded, in the cabinet and on the agent's home, in one line. "Leads can see your replies and your resolution times." Then make sure the first screen still rewards the next true reply, not the fastest close.

A trainee shadowing a thread should be a viewer with a name, not a shared login. Shared logins destroy the audit line you needed the day a refund went out. Seats are cheaper than that incident. The permission model can say so without a lecture: one person, one seat, the actions on the composer matching that seat.

## Write the boundary on the screen

For each action a reasonable agent will seek, choose show-with-reason or hide-because-it-would-be-nonsense. Reply, note, assign, refund, reopen, see payment, edit a shared snippet, connect a mailbox. Reply is never nonsense for an agent, so a trainee's missing send must be explained. Connecting a mailbox is nonsense for an agent, so it can live in the admin cabinet without a ghost button in the composer.

Check the server anyway. A polite screen over a wide-open refund endpoint is not a permission model. The screen and the action should tell the same story, so a modified client cannot do what the button refused.

On a Hanabi project we write the role sentences first, then the locked composer and the locked refund in Figma beside the open ones. The product is built in Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Seats, roles, and the conversation live in PostgreSQL via Prisma, so "who may refund" is a query you can read, not a flag sprinkled through components. Tailwind keeps notes and public replies obviously different. That visual difference is part of the permission, because a note sent by mistake is a permissions incident.

When an agent cannot find the conversation, the customer, or the old ticket, they will search. [Search inside a support inbox](/blog/search-inside-a-support-inbox) is the next piece. Search has to honor the same roles, and it has to be obvious when a thread is missing because it is out of scope rather than gone.

If you are unsure which actions your agents should even see, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of things a new hire tried to tap on their first day. That list is the permissions spec.
